prompt.adult: When the LORD began to give Ezekiel his commission, He called him “Son of man.” What did He tell Ezekiel to do before He spoke to him (2:1)?
prompt.child: God was about to give Ezekiel his work. What was the first thing God told him to do?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 2:1 opens Ezekiel’s call with a command, and 2:2 says the Spirit helped him obey it. What was the command?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 2:1, what did the LORD command Ezekiel to do so that He could speak to him?

verses.text: And He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak to you.”
Then the Spirit entered me when He spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard Him who spoke to me.

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 2:1 quotes the LORD. Read the words right after “Son of man,” before “and I will speak to you.”
explanation.child: Look at Ezekiel 2:1. God calls him “Son of man” and then gives a short command. Ezekiel 2:2 shows the Spirit helping him do it.
explanation.teen: 2:1 gives the command and 2:2 shows it carried out by the Spirit. Read what the Spirit did to Ezekiel in 2:2.
explanation.older: The command sits between “Son of man” and “and I will speak to you” in 2:1; 2:2 repeats it in action.

teaching.extended_explanation: In 2:1 the LORD addresses him as “Son of man” and gives a command before He speaks to him. In 2:2 the Spirit enters Ezekiel and does for him what he had been told to do, and then Ezekiel hears the One speaking. Read the command in 2:1 and the end of 2:2.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD said, “Son of man, stand on your feet,” and the Spirit set him on his feet.

prompt.adult: The LORD sent Ezekiel to a rebellious house and told him to speak whether they would hear or refuse. According to 2:5, what would they know either way?
prompt.child: God told Ezekiel that the people might listen or might not. Either way, what did God say they would know?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 2:5 and 2:7 repeat “whether they hear or whether they refuse.” What does 2:5 say the people will know in any case?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 2:5, what would the rebellious house know, whether they heard or refused?

choices.text: That the LORD had left His temple for good
That a prophet has been among them
That their exile was over at last

verses.text: As for them, whether they hear or whether they refuse—for they are a rebellious house—yet they will know that a prophet has been among them.
You shall speak My words to them, whether they hear or whether they refuse, for they are rebellious.

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 2:5 ends with “yet they will know.” Read the words that follow.
explanation.child: Look at the end of Ezekiel 2:5. After “yet they will know,” God tells what the people will know.
explanation.teen: 2:7 repeats the command to speak no matter what. In 2:5, read the clause after “yet they will know.”
explanation.older: The last clause of 2:5, after “yet they will know,” states it.

teaching.extended_explanation: The LORD did not promise Ezekiel that the people would listen. In 2:5 and again in 2:7 He says Ezekiel must speak His words whether they hear or whether they refuse, for they are a rebellious house. The end of 2:5 says what they would know either way. Read the clause after “yet they will know.”
teaching.takeaway: Whether they listened or refused, they would know that a prophet had been among them.

prompt.adult: A hand held out a scroll written inside and out with lamentations and mourning and woe (2:9-10). According to 3:1, what did the LORD tell Ezekiel to do with the scroll before going to speak to Israel?
prompt.child: God showed Ezekiel a scroll with sad words written all over it. What did God tell Ezekiel to do with it?
prompt.teen: Before Ezekiel speaks to the house of Israel, the LORD gives him a command about the scroll in 3:1. What is it?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 3:1-2, what was Ezekiel told to do with the scroll?

choices.text: Read it aloud in the gate

verses.text: Moreover He said to me, “Son of man, eat what you find; eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.”
So I opened my mouth, and He caused me to eat that scroll.

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 3:1 gives a two-part command about the scroll. Read the first part, right after “Son of man.”
explanation.child: Look at Ezekiel 3:1 and 3:2. God tells Ezekiel what to do with the scroll, and 3:2 says Ezekiel did it.
explanation.teen: 3:1 is the command and 3:2 is the obedience. Read the end of 3:2.
explanation.older: The command about the scroll is in the middle of 3:1, and 3:2 confirms it.

teaching.extended_explanation: In 2:8 the LORD tells Ezekiel not to be rebellious like the house of Israel. A hand holds out a scroll full of lamentations and mourning and woe (2:9-10). In 3:1 the LORD says what to do with it before Ezekiel goes to speak, and 3:2 says Ezekiel obeyed. Read the first command in 3:1.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD told Ezekiel to eat the scroll, and then go and speak to the house of Israel.

prompt.adult: Israel used a proverb about the fathers eating sour grapes and the children’s teeth being set on edge (18:2). What did the LORD declare instead in 18:4?
prompt.child: People in Israel had a saying that children suffer for what their parents did. What did God say instead?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 18:2 quotes a popular proverb, and the LORD rejects it. What principle does 18:4 state?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 18:4, what did the LORD say in place of the sour grapes proverb?

choices.text: The son shall bear his father’s sin
Every soul shall be spared alike
The land shall pay for every sin
The soul who sins shall die

verses.text: “What do you mean when you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, And the children’s teeth are set on edge’?
“Behold, all souls are Mine; The soul of the father As well as the soul of the son is Mine; The soul who sins shall die.

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 18:4 says all souls belong to the LORD. Read the last line of the verse.
explanation.child: Look at the end of Ezekiel 18:4. After God says every soul is His, the last line states the principle.
explanation.teen: 18:2 is the proverb; 18:4 is the LORD’s reply. Read the final line of 18:4.
explanation.older: The principle is the closing line of 18:4; 18:20 repeats it.

teaching.extended_explanation: The proverb in 18:2 claimed that children were paying for their fathers’ sins. In 18:3 the LORD says they will no longer use it. In 18:4 He says all souls are His, the father’s and the son’s alike, and the last line states the principle that the rest of chapter 18 explains with examples of a father and son (18:5-20). Read the final line of 18:4.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD said, “The soul who sins shall die,” not the children for the fathers.

prompt.adult: In the LORD’s picture, a watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet to warn the people (33:3). According to 33:5, what happens to the one who takes warning?
prompt.child: God described a watchman who blows a trumpet when an enemy is coming. What happens to the person who listens to the warning?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 33:3-5 describes a watchman’s trumpet and two kinds of listeners. What does 33:5 say about the one who takes warning?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 33:5, what will the one who takes warning do?

choices.text: He would be made a watchman
He would have to leave the land
He would face the sword alone

verses.text: when he sees the sword coming upon the land, if he blows the trumpet and warns the people,
He heard the sound of the trumpet, but did not take warning; his blood shall be upon himself. But he who takes warning will save his life.

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 33:5 has two parts, joined by “But.” Read the part after “But he who takes warning.”
explanation.child: Look at the end of Ezekiel 33:5. After “But he who takes warning,” the verse says what happens to him.
explanation.teen: 33:3 is the trumpet. 33:5 contrasts the one who ignores it with the one who heeds it. Read the last clause.
explanation.older: The result follows “But he who takes warning” at the end of 33:5.

teaching.extended_explanation: The LORD describes a watchman chosen by the people of a land. When he sees the sword coming, he blows the trumpet (33:3). Whoever hears and does not take warning is responsible for what happens to him (33:4-5). The end of 33:5 tells what happens to the one who does take warning. In 33:7 the LORD applies the picture to Ezekiel. Read the last clause of 33:5.
teaching.takeaway: The one who takes warning when the trumpet sounds will save his life.

prompt.adult: The LORD told Ezekiel that the house of Israel would not listen to him, because they would not listen to the LORD (3:7). According to 3:9, what had the LORD made Ezekiel’s forehead like?
prompt.child: God warned Ezekiel that the people would not listen to him. How did God say He had made Ezekiel’s forehead?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 3:7 describes Israel’s refusal to listen, and 3:8-9 describe how the LORD prepared Ezekiel to face them. What is Ezekiel’s forehead like in 3:9?
prompt.older: According to Ezekiel 3:9, what had the LORD made Ezekiel’s forehead like?

verses.text: But the house of Israel will not listen to you, because they will not listen to Me; for all the house of Israel are impudent and hard-hearted.
Like adamant stone, harder than flint, I have made your forehead; do not be afraid of them, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.”

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 3:9 begins with a comparison before “I have made your forehead.” Read the first line.
explanation.child: Look at the start of Ezekiel 3:9. It begins with a comparison.
explanation.teen: 3:7 is the people’s refusal; 3:9 is God’s reply. Read the words after “Like adamant stone.”
explanation.older: The comparison opens 3:9, before “I have made your forehead.”

teaching.extended_explanation: The LORD did not hide how difficult Ezekiel’s work would be. In 3:7 He says the house of Israel will not listen to Ezekiel because they will not listen to the LORD. In 3:8 He says He has made Ezekiel’s face and forehead strong against theirs, and 3:9 gives a comparison, then tells Ezekiel not to be afraid of them. Read the opening line of 3:9.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD made Ezekiel’s forehead like adamant stone, harder than flint, so he would not be afraid.

prompt.adult: Twice in Ezekiel 18 the house of Israel says, “The way of the Lord is not fair” (18:25, 29). What does the LORD reply is really not fair?
prompt.child: The people of Israel complained two times that God was not being fair. What did God say was the thing that was not fair?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 18:25 and 18:29 repeat the same complaint and the same reply. According to the LORD, what is not fair?
prompt.older: In Ezekiel 18:25 and 18:29, what does the LORD say is not fair?

verses.text: “Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Hear now, O house of Israel, is it not My way which is fair, and your ways which are not fair?
Yet the house of Israel says, ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ O house of Israel, is it not My ways which are fair, and your ways which are not fair?

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 18:25 ends with a question from the LORD. Read the last few words, after “is it not My way which is fair, and.”
explanation.child: Look at the end of Ezekiel 18:25. God asks a question that compares His way with something else. Read the end of that question.
explanation.teen: The complaint and reply appear in both 18:25 and 18:29. Read the second half of the LORD’s question in each.
explanation.older: The reply ends both 18:25 and 18:29, after “and.”

teaching.extended_explanation: Ezekiel 18 says the wicked who turn will live, and the righteous who turn away will die (18:21-28). The people complain that this is not fair. Twice the LORD answers with the same question, setting His way beside someone else’s. Read the last words of 18:25 and 18:29.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD said His way is fair, and it was their own ways that were not fair.

prompt.adult: The LORD made Ezekiel a watchman to warn the wicked to turn from his way (33:7-9). According to 18:32, why does the LORD call people to turn?
prompt.child: God made Ezekiel a watchman whose job was to warn people to turn from doing wrong. In Ezekiel 18:32, what reason does God give for calling people to turn?
prompt.teen: Ezekiel 33:7-9 sets out the watchman’s duty to warn. Ezekiel 18:32 gives a reason for the call to turn. What is it?
prompt.older: Compare Ezekiel 33:7-9 with 18:32. What reason does the Lord GOD give for His call to turn?

choices.text: He wants the watchman to be honored by all
He needs more servants in Israel
He plans to rebuild the temple soon
He takes no pleasure in their death

verses.text: “So you, son of man: I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; therefore you shall hear a word from My mouth and warn them for Me.
Nevertheless if you warn the wicked to turn from his way, and he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your soul.
For I have no pleasure in the death of one who dies,” says the Lord GOD. “Therefore turn and live!”

explanation.adult: Ezekiel 18:32 begins with “For.” Read the first clause, up to “says the Lord GOD.”
explanation.child: Look at the start of Ezekiel 18:32. God gives His reason before He says “Therefore turn.”
explanation.teen: 33:7-9 is the watchman’s task. In 18:32, read the clause before “says the Lord GOD,” then the command that follows.
explanation.older: The reason is the opening clause of 18:32; “Therefore” links it to the command.

teaching.extended_explanation: In 33:7 the LORD makes Ezekiel a watchman who must hear a word from His mouth and warn the people for Him. In 33:9, if Ezekiel warns the wicked to turn and he does not, Ezekiel has delivered his soul. The warning is not the LORD’s last word, though. Ezekiel 18:30-32 calls Israel to repent and get a new heart, and 18:32 gives the LORD’s own reason before the command “Therefore turn and live!” Read the first clause of 18:32.
teaching.takeaway: The watchman warned because the LORD has no pleasure in the death of one who dies; He calls people to turn and live.
